en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiji of Yangshan in Yuanzhou,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Yufeng Yuanshin of Mount Jing,
with Guo Ningzhi serving as the editor-in-chief.
The Master’s taboo name was Huaiji; he was the son of the Ye family of Huaihua in Shaoyou Prefecture.
At the age of nine, he entered the Sangha under Chan Master Tong at He’an Temple in Guangzhou, whereupon he immediately ceased speaking to him.
At the age of fourteen, his parents took him home, intending to arrange a marriage for him.

The Master would not comply; they consequently cut off two of his fingers, whereupon he knelt before his parents and vowed to seek the True Dharma as a repayment for their labor. His parents then consented, and he went once more to the monastery to receive the tonsure.
Before he had even received full ordination, he began his travels.
Initially, he visited Master Danyuan and already realized the profound essence; later, he studied under Master Weishan and eventually entered the inner sanctum.
Master Danyuan said to him:
"The National Teacher at that time received seventy-nine *yuanxiang* (circular diagrams) from the Sixth Patriarch; he transmitted them to me, saying:
'Thirty years after my passing, a śrāmaṇera shall come from the south to greatly propagate this teaching. You must transmit it in succession so that it does not become extinct.'"
"I now entrust this to you; you should uphold it.
He then took the original manuscript and presented it to his teacher. Upon receiving it, the teacher glanced over it once and then burned it with fire.
One day, Tanyuan asked,
"The various signs that appeared previously were quite worthy of being kept secret.
The Master said:
Danyuan said, "At that time, you saw it and immediately burned it.
No one can understand this Dharma-gate of mine; only my former teacher, the various patriarchs, and the great sages can fully comprehend it. How could you burn it?"
The Master said, "Huiji understood the meaning upon a single glance; however, one must apply it in practice and not cling to the source text.
Danyuan said:
"Even so, while you may have attained it, future generations will not be able to believe it.
The Master said,
"If the Abbot wishes for it, it would not be difficult to record it again."
He immediately compiled another copy and presented it, with nothing further omitted.
Danyuan said, "Indeed."
When Danyuan ascended the hall, the Master stepped forward from the assembly and drew this ○-shaped mudra; having displayed it with his hand, he then stood with his hands folded.
Danyuan crossed both hands and made a fist to show him, whereupon the Master stepped forward three paces and performed a woman’s bow.
Danyuan nodded his head, and the Master then prostrated.
While the Master was washing his cassock, Danyuan said,
"At such a time as this, what do you do?"
The Master said:
"At such a time as this, where do you see it?
Later, he visited Mount Gui, and Mount Gui asked:
"Are you a novice with a master,
or a novice without a master?
The Master said:
"There is a master. Muzhou said, "Where is the master?"
The Master walked from west to east and stood there.
Guishan was struck by this and asked:
"What is the dwelling place of the true Buddha?

Guishan replied, "By means of the wondrous state where thought is without thinking, one turns back upon the infinite brilliance of spiritual awareness. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source; nature and characteristics abide eternally, and phenomena and principle are non-dual—the true Buddha is suchness."
Upon these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment; from then on, he attended [Baizhang] and remained in his service for fifteen years.
While the Master was sweeping the floor, Guishan asked:
"Dust is not something that can be swept away, and space does not arise of itself."
"What is this dust that cannot be swept away?
The Master swept the floor once.
Guishan said:
"How is it that emptiness does not arise of itself?
The Master pointed to himself and then pointed to Moshan.
Moshan said:
"Dust cannot be swept away, and emptiness does not arise of itself.
Apart from these two paths, how would you do it?
The Master swept the ground once more, then pointed to himself and pointed to Muzhou Daoyuan.
One day, Guishan pointed to a field and asked the Master,
"In this field, which end is high and which end is low?
The Master replied:
"It is simply that this end is high and that end is low.
Guishan said,
"If you do not believe me, stand in the middle and look at both ends."
The Master said:
"There is no need to stand in the middle, nor should you dwell at either end.
Guishan said:
"If it is so, try placing it in water and observing; water can level things.
The Master said, "Water has no fixed nature either; it simply levels what is high by being high and levels what is low by being low."
Thus, Guishan ceased speaking.
A donor once presented silk to Guishan,
and the Master asked:
“The Master has received such offerings from a donor; how will you repay them?
Guishan struck the meditation seat to indicate his answer.
The Master said:
"How can you, Preceptor, take the property of the assembly and use it for your own purposes?
Another version states that Guishan asked the Master:
"A lay disciple brought three bundles of silk to redeem the bell for me; thus, I am receiving blessings from worldly people."
The Master said,
"If the lay disciple gives silk to the Abbot to redeem the bell, what will you, Abbot, offer him in return?
Guishan struck the meditation seat three times with his staff and said:
"I will repay him with this," [the student] said.
The Master said, "If it is this, what would you do with it?"
Guishan struck the meditation seat three more times and said,
"Why do you dislike this?
The Master replied:
"Such-and-such does not begrudge this; it simply belongs to everyone.
Guishan said, "Since you know it belongs to everyone, why do you still come to me to seek goods to repay him?"
The Master said,
"I only resent you, Preceptor, for handling the affairs of others on behalf of everyone.
Guishan said:
"Do you not see that Master Dharma came here from the Western Heaven, bringing this very object as a gift for people?
All of you are simply recipients of his offerings."
The Master was at Mount Guiyang serving as the *zhisui* (steward) when he returned from his labors.
Mount Guiyang asked him, "Where have you been?"
The Master said,
"Come from the field. Muzhou said:
“How many people are in the field?
The Master thrust his hoe into the ground and stood with his hands clasped behind his back.
Guishan said:
"Today there are many people on the South Mountain cutting thatch.
The Master pulled up his spade and departed.
Xuansha Bei said:
"If I were to see it, I would immediately kick over the spade.
A monk asked Jingqing,
"What was the meaning of Yangshan planting his spade?"
Jingqing said:
"A dog bites a royal pardon; the feudal lords clear the way.
The monk asked:
"If Xuansha simply trod him down, what was his underlying meaning?
Jingqing said,
"When the boat cannot be saved, one breaks the scoop."
The monk asked,
"Regarding 'cutting the thatch in the South Mountain,' what is the underlying meaning?
Jingqing said:
"Lǐ Jìng, the third elder brother, has long experienced the ranks of battle.
Yúnjū Xī said, "But tell me,
when Jingqing made this judgment, was he on the mark?"
"Not attached?
Xuedou Xian said, "Everywhere it is said that the 'Plowing with a Hoe' story is extraordinary; this is much like following the heterodox and pursuing evil."
According to Xuedou’s perspective, when Yangshan was questioned by Guishan, he was so thoroughly bound by his own straw ropes that he was as good as dead.
Cuiyan Zhi said:
"Yangshan only managed to get one peg; do you all have another way of understanding this?"
When the Master was herding oxen at Mount Gui, the Venerable Tiantai asked him:
"I do not ask about a single-hair lion appearing;
but when ten billion hairs appear as ten billion lions, what then?"
The Master then mounted his ox and returned.
While he was standing in attendance beside Guishan, just as he finished recounting the previous conversation, he saw Xitai approaching.
The Master said:
"This is that very person, the Senior Monk (Upādhyāya)," said [the attendant].
Baizhang then asked, "A billion lions appear from every pore; is this not what you, the Senior Monk, have spoken?"
Tai said, "Yes. The Master said:
"At this very moment, does the hair appear before or after?
Tai said:
“I do not speak of before or after at this moment,” Baizhang said.
Miaoshan laughed loudly.
The Master said:
"The Lion’s waist has broken," he said, and then descended.

As the Master followed Guishan on a mountain excursion, they reached a large flat rock where Guishan sat. While the Master stood in attendance, a crow suddenly dropped a red persimmon before him; Guishan picked it up and gave it to the Master.
The Master received it, washed it, and passed it to Guishan.
Guishan asked,
"Where did you get this?"
The Master said,
"This is moved by the virtue of the Abbot.
Guishan said:
"You shall not be without your share," he said,
and immediately divided half [of it] and gave it to his teacher.
Xuan Sha said:
“Both the Great and Small Miaoshan were pinned down by Yangshan’s single sitting; even until now, they cannot rise.
Miaoshan asked the Master, “If someone were to ask you this, how would you respond?”
The Master said,
"If the Master of Dongsi, my uncle, were here, I would not be left in such solitude. Guishan said:
"I release you from one offense for which you have not yet made amends.
The Master said,
"Life and death depend upon a single word."
Taisu said, "I do not fail you in your insight; others simply would not agree.
The Master said:
"Who is it? Guishan pointed to a pillar and said, "This one."
The Master said,
"What did you say? Guishan replied:
"What did you say? The Master replied,
"The white rat moves on, yet the silver terrace remains unchanged."
The Master asked Guishan, “When the great function manifests before you, I ask you, Master, to discern and clarify it.
Guishan descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters; the Master followed him in.
Guishan asked,
"What was the question you were just asking?
The Master raised the matter again.
Guishan said,
"Do you still remember my answer?
The Master said:
"I remember it," said Guishan.
"Try reciting it for me."
The Master then took his leave with deep respect.
Guishan said,
"A mistake."
The Master turned his head and said,
"If the junior brother Xian comes, do not say that I have nothing to say.
While the Master was herding oxen on the front slope of Mount Guiyang, he saw a monk who had gone up the mountain and soon came back down.
The Master then asked,
"Why do you not remain in the mountains for a while, Senior Monk?
The monk replied:
"It is simply because the causal conditions do not accord.
The Master asked,
"What are those causal conditions?"
"Try citing one for me," he said.
The monk replied,
"When the Master asked me what my name was, I answered, 'Returning to Truth' (Guizhen)."
The Master said,
"Where is the returning to truth? I had no reply.
The Master said:
"Return, Senior Monk, and tell the Abbot: 'I have spoken.'"
The Preceptor asked,
"How do you say it? He simply said:
"Within the eye, within the ear, within the nose.
The monk turned around exactly as instructed.
Guishan said:
"The man who speaks empty, deceptive words—these are the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of five hundred people.
While the Master was lying down, he dreamed that he entered the assembly hall of Maitreya’s inner court; all the seats were filled except for the second one, so the Master took his seat there.
An elder struck the gavel and said,
"Now the second seat shall preach the Dharma.
The Master rose and struck the gavel, saying:
“The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; listen attentively, listen attentively!
Upon saying this, the assembly all dispersed.
When [Nanquan] awoke, he related this to Guishan, who said:
"You have already entered the rank of the sages.
The Master then bowed.
Wuyue Xiu said:
"It is not that interpreting the meaning based on the text is entirely without merit;
however, if there were suddenly someone in Maitreya’s assembly who, upon hearing the words 'Mahāyāna Dharma,' immediately said:
'Shut your two flaps of skin!'"
"Not only does this stop the 'sleep-talk' of Yangshan, it also prevents later generations from dreaming about dreams.
Langye Huijue said:
"Tell me, do the holy assembly approve of Yangshan, or do they disapprove of him?"
If you agree, you will again be failing Yangshan;
if you do not agree, Yangshan is like someone tripping on level ground.
Today, this mountain monk will not spare his eyebrows to explain it through for you all:
The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
If you were to present this to those in various quarters, and they were to understand it in such a way, they would enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Dongchan Guan said:

"When the Venerable One struck the gavel, the assembly of holy ones dispersed; this leaves people with lingering doubts. Only after they have been splashed with a second ladle of foul water will they finally awaken."
"Furthermore, for instance, the Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; the Way has already been realized. Do you all still recognize Yangshan?
While the Master was walking with Guishan, he suddenly saw dust rising ahead.
Guishan asked, "What is this before you?
The Master stepped forward, looked at it, and then made this gesture; Guishan nodded his head.
Guishan addressed the assembly, saying:
"All sentient beings have no Buddha-nature.
Yanguan addressed the assembly, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Two monks from Yanguan went there to inquire; having arrived at Mount Wei, they heard Wei’s teachings being proclaimed, but finding them unfathomable, they conceived feelings of contempt.
One day, while conversing with his teacher, [Dongshan] exhorted him, saying, "Brother, you must study diligently;
the Buddha-dharma is not to be taken lightly.
The teacher then made this ○-shaped gesture, presenting it with his hand and then throwing it behind his back, before spreading both hands out toward the two monks as if requesting something.
The two monks were at a loss for words.
The Master said, "My elder brother must study diligently; the Buddha-dharma is not to be taken lightly."
He then rose and departed.
At that time, the two monks returned to Yanguan. After traveling thirty li, one monk suddenly attained realization and said:
"One should know that when Baizhang said, 'All sentient beings have no Buddha-nature,' his words were correct."
He then returned to Mount Gui.
Another monk continued on for several more *li*; while crossing a stream, he suddenly attained realization and sighed to himself, saying:
"Mount Gui said, 'All sentient beings have no Buddha-nature. It is truly remarkable that he spoke in such a way."
He also returned to Mount Gui, where he remained for a long time in attendance at the Dharma seat.

Because several people from the assembly at Yanguan refused to submit to him at Mount Gui, one day while they were working together (*pǔqǐng*) transporting rice stalks to the western fields, the Master reached the top of a ridge and set his load down; subsequently, ten or so other people also arrived and set their loads down.
The Master then lifted up the bamboo grain basket, walked once around the assembly, and said:
"Is there anyone?
Is there anyone?"
The monk who had come alone did not respond.
The Master said,
"He has brought disaster upon himself."
He then shouldered the grain and departed.
While Guishan was herding oxen together with his master, Guishan asked,
"Is there still a bodhisattva here?"
The Master said,
"There is. Guishan said:
The Master said, "Which one do you see as being correct? Try to point it out.
The teacher replied, "Which one does the Abbot suspect is incorrect? Try to point it out."
Dongshan then desisted.
The Master presented some fruit to Guishan; Guishan accepted it and asked, "Where did you get this?"
The Master said,
"The very foundation of the family garden. Guishan said:
"Are you able to eat it yet?
The Master said, "I have not yet dared to taste it; first I offer it to the Venerable."
Taisu said, "Whose is it? The Master replied:
"Your wisdom is profound and still.
Miaoshan said, "Since it is yours, why do you ask me to taste it first?"
The Master said,
"The Abbot has tasted it a thousand times and ten thousand times.
Baizhang then ate it and said:
"It still retains a trace of sourness and astringency.
The Master said,
"Is this sourness and astringency not known by yourself?"
Guishan did not answer.
At the end of the summer retreat, as the Master was paying his respects to Guishan, Guishan said, "I have not seen you for an entire summer; what have you been doing down there?"
The Master said,
"I have cleared a patch of fallow land down below and sown a basketful of seed.
Guishan said:
"You have not spent this summer in vain,
my son," the Master replied. He then asked,
"I wonder, what were your activities during this summer retreat?"
Taisu said, "One meal at midday; one sleep after midnight.
The Master said:
“Master, you too have not spent this summer in vain.
Having said this, he stuck out his tongue.
Guishan said:
"Jizang, how could you harm your own life? Wuquan Zhe said:
"Yangshan’s eye illuminates the four quarters of the world, yet upon reaching the presence of Dayuan, he tumbles down on the pure ground."
Daguan may be called the karmic condition for raising a son, yet he cannot avoid being on the lips and teeth of later generations.
Longmen Yuan said:
“When Master Miu and his son Yang met in their daily lives, their playful exercise of spiritual powers was no small matter; is there anyone who can truly know this?”
If there were none, this mountain monk would explain it for you all.
Once a patch of fallow land has been cleared—continuous and dense—the Way will naturally be accomplished with two meals of congee.
This mountain monk has been in audience with you all this summer, yet it is simply because you have failed to realize it.
If you were to realize it as a single whole, what would that one piece be?
"Look at the arrow pointing directly at the gate. Xichan Ru said:

"Master Miu and his son were able to enter and exit, to roll up and unroll [the teachings], with complete mastery. You all must not deliberate upon this as mundane worldly truth, nor must you interpret it as a matter of Buddhist Dharma."
Since you are not permitted at all to deliberate in such a manner, how, in the end, can one understand it?
Having cleared a patch of slash-and-burn field and sown a basketful of millet, one turns the head for a leisurely glance: the mountains are green and the waters are lush again.
All day long there is but one meal; after nightfall, there is but one sleep. When weariness comes, one sleeps on one’s side—thousandfold and ten-thousandfold contentment.
As the eighth and ninth months draw near, yellow chrysanthemums spread profusely by the hedge.
Donglin Yan said:
"Nowadays, monks gather in groups of hundreds and thousands; passing through winter and summer, they waste their years in vain, which is a profound insult to the ancients."
"East Lin did not examine the former sages; Yangshan displayed his brilliance too much, and his sticking out his tongue only achieved half the mark.

The Master likewise crossed his two hands, each giving three flicks, then brought them to his chest; with one hand turned upward and the other downward, he gazed with his eyes.

The Master said,
"As for this matter of great significance, how would you go about testing it?"
Guishan held up his fist.
The Master said,
"In the end, this is merely pointing east and drawing west."
Taisu said, "What was it you were just now asking?
The Master said:
“[The student] asked about the great matter of the Master’s causal conditions. Baizhang said,
“Why do you call this ‘pointing east and drawing west’?”
The Master said,
"It is because you are attached to sounds and forms that I have questioned you,
O So-and-so. Guishan said:
"I have not yet understood this matter.
The Master said,
"How can you come to understand this matter?"
Taisu said, "Jizi’s sounds and forms are this old monk’s coming and going.
The Master said:
"In a thousand rivers in one month, the substance of the water is not divided.
Guishan said,
"One must be like this before it can be attained."
The Master said:
"It is like gold and gold; ultimately there is no difference in color—how could there be different names?
Guishan said:
"What is the principle of that which has no different names?
The Master said:
"A jar, a platter, hairpins, bracelets, a bond, a basin, and a tub."
Tianping said, "Jizi’s preaching of Chan is like the roar of a lion, startling and dispersing the foxes, wolves, and jackals.
One day, while the Master was attending upon Guishan, he suddenly heard the singing of birds. Guishan said:

He suddenly snatched it away and smashed it.
Later, during the monks' formal visit, he asked:
"Does the Master recognize characters?"
The Master said, “According to one’s lot.
The monk drew this ○ symbol with his hand and presented it; the Master brushed it away with his sleeve.
The monk again made this ○-shaped mudrā and presented it; the Master made a gesture with both hands as if tossing something behind his back.
The monk looked at him with his eyes, and the Master lowered his head.
The monk circumambulated the Master once, and the Master struck him; the monk then departed.
While the Master was seated, a monk came forward to pay his respects, but the Master did not look at him.
The monk then asked,
"Does the Master recognize characters?"
The Master said,
"According to one's lot.
He then turned once to the right and said:
"What character is this?
The Master wrote the character "十" (ten) on the ground in response.
The monk then circled it once counter-clockwise and said:
“What character is this?
The Master changed the ten characters into the *svastika* (卍).
The monk drew this ○ symbol and, with both hands pressed against it, assumed the posture of an asura grasping the sun and moon, saying:
"What character is this?
The Master then drew this [symbol] facing him.
The monk then made the gesture of *Louzhide* (the "Laozi" seal), whereupon the Master said:
"It is so, it is so; this is that which all Buddhas protectively mind. You are likewise, and I am likewise; you must skillfully protect and maintain it yourself."
The monk bowed in thanks and departed, soaring through the air.
At that time, a practitioner witnessed this; five days later, he questioned the Master.
The Master said:
"Do you see him return?
The practitioner replied,
"I saw him leave the gate and ascend into the air."
The Master said,
"This is an Arhat from Western Heaven who has come specifically to investigate my Way.
The practitioner said:
"Although I have witnessed various samādhis, I do not discern their underlying principle.
The Master said,
"I shall explain them for you according to their meaning:"
These are the eight kinds of samādhi; they are the ocean of awakening transformed into the ocean of meaning, their essence being identical.
This meaning comprises both cause and fruit, whether simultaneous or sequential, and in its general and particular aspects, it is not separate from the samādhi of invisibility.

A Brahman monk came to visit the Master. The Master drew the shape of a half-moon on the ground; the monk stepped forward, added to it to make a full circle, and then appeared to wipe away the mark with his foot.
The Master spread his two hands; the monk brushed his sleeves and departed.
The Master asked the monk, "Where have you recently come from?"
[The monk] said, “The south.
The Master raised his staff and said:
“Did that elder there also speak of this? He replied, “He did not.”
The Master said,
"If you do not speak of this, do you perhaps speak of that?
He replied:
"I will not speak.
The Master called out,
"Virtuous One!"
The assembly responded, "Yes.
The Master said,
"Go to the hall for practice."
The assembly then departed.
The Master called out again, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!"
The assembly turned their heads.
The Master said,
"Come forward."
The monk approached; the Master struck him once with the tip of his staff and said, "Go!
Yunmen Wenyan then remarked:
"If Yangshan had not had those subsequent words, how could one have recognized the man?

One day, as the Master sat in the Dharma Hall, he saw a monk coming from outside; after the monk had paid his respects, he stood with his hands folded at his chest toward the east, looking at the Master. The Master then lowered his left foot.
The monk then moved to the west side and stood with his hands folded, whereupon the Master lowered his right foot.
The monk stood with his hands joined at his chest toward the center; the Master drew in both feet.
The monk prostrated, and the Master said, "Since I have resided here, I have never struck a single person."
He raised his staff and struck him; the monk then soared into the air and departed.
The Master pointed to a snow lion and asked the assembly, "Is there anyone who can pass through this form?"
The assembly had no reply.
Yunmen said:
"At that moment, one should have simply pushed him over."
Xuedou Xian said:
"Yunmen only knows how to knock someone over; he does not know how to help them up.
While the Master was lying down, a monk asked him:
“Does the Dharmakāya also expound the Dharma?
The Master said, “I cannot expound it; there is another person who can.”
[The Master] asked,
"Where is the person who can speak thus?
The Master pushed out his pillow.
When Guishan heard this, he said,
"Jizi is employing the business of the sword's edge.
Jingshan Daokai said:

“Guishan was truly like a parent who, out of love for their child, fails to notice their ugliness; Yangshan’s pushing out the pillow was already a betrayal, yet he further gave it a name, calling it ‘the matter on the edge of a sword,’ misleading those who merely mimic the words of others so that they might pass it along in this way, receiving echoes in empty space.”
Although Miaoxi borrowed water to offer flowers, fundamentally there was no deviation or contradiction in principle; yet, does anyone here now come forward with a refusal?
I wish to ask you: when you pushed out the pillow, did that truly constitute the Dharma-body preaching the Dharma?
Tiantong Hua said:
"If this were a matter of sword-blades, how could Jizi have ever known how to use them?
Suppose a monk were to come forward and ask, 'Does the Dharmakāya understand how to preach the Dharma? One should tell him: 'I cannot say it; there is another person who can.'"
He asked again, "Where is the person who has attained it? Yunmen replied to him, "Three lives, sixty kalpas.
Lingyin Yue said, "Yangshan’s backbone had been as hard as iron all along, but having been pressed by this monk time and again, its four corners have now collapsed to the ground."
Taisu could not restrain his impatience for a moment, unaware that he had lost one of his eyes.

Suddenly, a monk asked Yefu, "Does the Dharma-body know how to preach the Dharma? Yefu immediately gave him a chest-thrusting kick, knocking him down, intending to make him rise up as a man who is free and unencumbered.
It is not said:
"The rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn from gazing at the moon; the elephant receives blossoms within its tusks from being startled by thunder.
While the Master sat with his eyes closed, a monk quietly approached and stood beside him.
The Master opened his eyes and drew this symbol on the ground; he looked at the monk, but the monk remained silent.
As the Master walked along carrying his staff, the monk asked:
"What is this in the Master's hand?
The Master then held it up behind his back and said,
"Do you see it?"
The assembly remained silent.
The Master asked one monk,
"What do you understand?"
[The Master] said,
"I understand divination.
The Master then raised his whisk and said:
"In which hexagram among the sixty-four is this one subsumed?
The monk had no reply.
The Master spoke on his behalf:
"Previously it was 'Thunder in Heaven: Great Strength' (Lèitiān Dàzhuàng); now it has changed into 'Earth and Fire:
Illumination in Obscurity' (Dìhuǒ Míngyí). He asked a monk, "What is its name?"
[The monk] said,
"Spiritual penetration.
The Master said:
He said, "Please enter the lantern.
[The Master] replied,
"I have already entered long ago."
Fayan said separately,
"What do you call a lantern?
He asked:
"An ancient said, 'When you see form, you see the mind. This meditation seat is form; please, Master, set aside the form and point out the mind of the student.
The Master said, "Which one is the meditation seat?"
"Point it out to me.
The monk had no reply.
Xuangjiao said:
“Suddenly he points his finger at the meditation seat; how would you respond to him?
A monk said, “I ask the Master to speak for me.”
Xuánjué, acting on his behalf, clapped his hands three times.
He asked:
"What is the Vairocana Teacher?"
The Master then rebuked him.
The monk asked,
"What is the Master's teacher?"
The Master said,
"Do not be discourteous.
While the Master was conversing with a monk, another monk standing nearby said:
"Speaking is Mañjuśrī; silence is Vimalakīrti.
The Master said, "Is it not you who neither speaks nor remains silent?"
The assembly remained silent.
The Master said,
"Why do you not manifest your supernatural powers?"
He said, "I do not decline to manifest spiritual powers; I only fear that the Master might categorize them as mere doctrine.
The Master said:
"I have examined where you come from, and you do not yet possess the eye that lies outside the teachings.
He asked:
"How far apart are heaven and hell?"
The Master took up his staff and drew a line on the ground.
When the Master was staying at Guanyin, he posted a notice that said:
"While reading the scriptures, one must not ask questions."
A monk came to pay his respects; seeing the Master reading a sutra, he stood to one side and waited.
The Master rolled up the sutra and asked, "Do you understand?"
[The monk] said,
"If I do not read the sutras, how can I understand them?
The Master said:
"You will see him again later.
That monk went to Yantou, and Yantou asked,
"Where have you come from?"
[The monk] said,
"Guanyin from Jiangxi has come.
Yantou said:
"What words did the Master have?
The monk recounted the previous conversation.
Yantou said:
"This master—I thought he had been buried under old scrolls, yet it turns out he is still here.
The monk Enxu asked:
"Regarding the sudden enlightenment of the Chan school, what is the fundamental meaning of entering the gate?"
The Master said:
"This meaning is extremely difficult.

If one belongs to the lineage of the Patriarchs, those of the highest faculties and supreme wisdom will attain awakening upon hearing it once, realizing a thousand insights and attaining great dhāraṇī."

"Those whose faculties are dull and whose wisdom is inferior, if they do not settle themselves in dhyāna and meditative concentration, will find themselves utterly bewildered upon reaching this point. He asked,
"Aside from this single path, is there another way of entry?"
The Master said,
“There is. He asked:
“How is it so? The Master said, “Where are you from?”
[The monk] said,
“A person from Youzhou.
The Master said:
"Do you still think of that place?
He replied,
"I constantly think of it."
The Master said:
"That which is capable of thinking is the mind; that which is thought of is the object.
As for those towers and pavilions, groves and gardens, people, horses, and crowds there—when you reflect upon the very basis of this, are there still so many varieties present?"
He said, "I have come here and do not see anything at all.
The Master said:
[The Master said: "Your understanding still resides in the mind; you have attained the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), but the stage of a person (*pudgala*) has not yet been reached.
[The student] asked: "Aside from this, is there any other meaning?"
The Master said:
"To say 'separately existent' or 'separately non-existent' is simply inadequate. He asked:
"Having arrived here, what is it?
The Master said, "According to your understanding, you have only attained one mystery; you may sit and don your robes, but look back for yourself later."
He bowed in thanks.
A monk asked:
"When the Tripitaka Master with Large Ears came for the third time, why did he not see the National Teacher?"
The Master said:
"The previous two instances were states of mind involving external objects; later, he entered the samādhi of self-enjoyment, which is why he did not see it.
Guishan asked the Master:
“Regarding the karmic conditions of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu, what was the intent of these two venerable masters?
The Master said,
“This was to manifest great capacity and great function.”
Tianyi Weishan said:
"Among the eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* that Mazu produced, how many attained the Great Functioning?
How many attained the Great Capacity?"
The Master said, "Baizhang attained the Great Functioning; Huangbo attained the Great Utility; all others were merely teachers of exhortation.
Guishan said:
"So it is, so it is. Guishan raised the story of Baizhang and the wild fox to question the Master.
The Master said:
"Huangbo often used this device.
Guishan said, "Tell me,
was it born of nature?"
"Is it obtained from others?
The Master said,
"It is both received through the lineage of a teacher and realized through the penetration of one's own nature."
Tianping said, "It is so, it is so.
Tianping then cited the instance where Baizhang asked Huangbo, "Where have you come from? to which Huangbo replied:
"I have come from picking chestnuts beneath Mount Daxiong.
Baizhang asked,
"Did you see the tiger?"
Huangbo then let out a tiger’s roar; Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture of striking. Huangbo then gave Baizhang a slap, whereupon Baizhang laughed heartily and departed.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Beneath Mount Daxiong there is a great beast; you all must watch out for it, for today this old fellow Baizhang has been personally caught by its mouth."
He asked the Master, "How is it?
The Master said:
"What about the Abbot?
Guishan said, "Baizhang should have struck him dead with a single axe then and there; why did things come to this?"
The Master said, "Not so. Guishan said:
"What do you say to this, my son?
The Master replied, "Baizhang only knows how to ride the tiger's head; he does not know how to grasp the tiger's tail."
Tiaoshan said,
"Your words contain a precipice.
Tiaoshan then cited Nanquan’s question to Huangbo:
"Regarding the equal training in concentration and wisdom that clearly perceives the Buddha-nature— how is this principle to be understood?
Huangbo replied,
"In the twelve periods of the day, do not rely upon or depend on a single thing."
Nanquan said,
"Is this not your own realization,
Elder? Huangbo said:
"I dare not. Nanquan said,
"Setting aside the payment for the rice gruel and water for a moment, who will repay the cost of the straw sandals?"
Huangbo stopped there.
The Master asked him,
"Is it not that Huangbo could not outwit Nanquan?"
The Master said, "Not so;
you must know that Huangbo possesses the trap for catching tigers.
Guishan said:
"Did you see how long he was when he arrived?
Once, while Huangbo was serving as the head seat under Nanquan, he took his alms bowl and sat in Nanquan’s place.
Nanquan entered the hall, saw him, and asked:
"Venerable sir,
in what year did you begin practicing the Way?"
Huangbo said,
"Before King Majestic Sound.
Nanquan said:
"This is still the lineage of our old teacher, the Master.
Huangbo then moved past the second seat and sat down; Nanquan then desisted.
Guishan said:
"One who deceives the enemy perishes.
The Master said: "Not so;
you must understand that Huangbo possesses the mechanism for trapping tigers."
Taisu said, "How far-reaching is your realization?
Taisu then cited Huangbo’s address to the assembly:
"All of you here are nothing but wine-dregs eaters; practicing *xunfu* like this, how could there be such a thing as 'today'?
Do you even know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no *chan-shi*?"
At that time, a monk said,
"As for those in various quarters who guide their disciples and lead the assembly,
how do they do it? Huangbo said:
"It is not that there is no dhyāna; it is simply that there is no teacher.
He asked the Master, "How is it?"
The Master said:
"The Goose King selects milk; he has never been of the same class as a duck.
Guishan said:

"It is truly difficult to discern [the truth] here; the Master and Disciple of the Miu-Oang lineage engaged in a vigorous exchange of challenges and evaluations, and their dialogues are numerous. Those that are already contained within the *Record of Linji* will not be recorded again here."
The Venerable Huo went to Baizhang because of this.
Baizhang said,
"Reverend, may I ask you something?"
Huangbo said, "Fortunately, it was not yet spoken; why the need for such idle chatter?
Baizhang said:
"Having secured Annam, one again worries about the north of the Great Wall.
Huo opened wide his chest and said, "Is it so?"
"Is it not so? Baizhang said, "In any case, it is difficult to grasp; in any case, it is difficult to grasp."
Huò said, "If you know, you have attained it; if you know, you have attained it.
The Master said:
"If there were someone who knew the whereabouts of these two men, it would be truly extraordinary.
If one cannot discern them, it is much like being lost in the middle of the day.
He then raised his five peaks and asked a monk:
“Where have you come from?
The monk replied,
“I have come from the village.”
Wufeng said, "Do you still see the ox?
The monk replied:
“I see it. Wufeng said,
“Do you see its left horn?”
"Do you see the right corner?
The monk was speechless.
Wufeng spoke on his behalf:
"I see no left or right.
The Master replied separately:
"Can you still distinguish left from right?"
There was a practitioner who followed the Dharma Master into the Buddha hall; the practitioner spat toward the Buddha.
The Dharma Master said:
"This practitioner lacks propriety; why did you spit at the Buddha?"
The practitioner said,
"I fear you have come from a place where there is no Buddha to spit upon me.
The Dharma Master had no reply.
Miaoshan said,
"The benevolent person is actually non-benevolent, and the non-benevolent person is actually benevolent.
The Master spoke on behalf of the Dharma Master, saying:
"Simply spit on the practitioner.
He further said:
"If the practitioner says anything, immediately say this to him:"
"Return to the place where there is no practice!

The Master took seizing the opportune moment to benefit sentient beings as his standard for the Gate of the Patriarchs. He later moved to Dongping; as he was about to pass into stillness, several monks stood in attendance, and the Master showed them this verse, saying:
"One, two, three, you disciples! Look down with level eyes, then look up again. Two mouths and not a single tongue— This is the very essence of my school."
At noon on that day, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly, and spoke again in verse:
"My years have reached seventy-seven; impermanence comes this very day. The sun is at its zenith at midday, as my two hands grasp my bent knees."
Having finished speaking, he passed away while cradling his knees with both hands.

The following year, Chan Master Nantaya Yong enshrined his remains at Mount Yang, interring them beneath Jiyun Peak and posthumously bestowing upon him the title "Chan Master Zhitong Miaoguang" and the memorial tower name "Miaoguang-ta."
